narrator.name: The Atlas narrator
narrator.voice: warm, unhurried, curious; a documentary voice that never oversells; speaks the dance's own words (names, counts) clearly
narrator.rule: The narrator only says what the profile says. Every sentence can be traced to a section, a claim or the music/movement DNA.
narrator.identity: one narrator for the whole atlas: the same face and animation everywhere; a native-speaker voice of the same character per language (studio-grade); the viewer chooses the language
narrator.wardrobe: in each episode the narrator wears the traditional apparel associated with the dance, reconstructed with meticulous care from the profile's costume notes and the licensed images — genuine and respectful, never a caricature; sacred, ceremonial or restricted attire is never worn (the narrator stays in neutral dress with a respectful nod in colour and fabric); the pack's visual_brief.wardrobe says which
narrator.languages: master narration in English; translations per language in episodes/i18n/<lang>/<slug>.json with the same scene structure (pipeline/translate.py); names, places and counts are never translated

narration: The Flea Hop: The High-Speed Energy of Collegiate Shag
This is Collegiate Shag. 1930s.

scenes.title: Where and when
narration: The dance originated in the African American community of the Carolinas in the 1920s.
It was initially a street dance before being standardized by the Arthur Murray studios in the late 1930s.
The name 'collegiate' was applied to distinguish it from other regional shag variations popular among the youth of the era.
on_screen: Map: United States · North America
Image — MISSING

scenes.title: When it is danced
narration: Originally a social dance for youth in the 1930s and 40s.
Today, it is practiced at swing dance festivals and social dance nights worldwide.
Today it is a living tradition.
on_screen: Footage: Collegiate Shag (Part 2): Jenni's Joint #16 (https://archive.org/details/Collegiate_Shag_Part_2_-_Jenni_s_Joint_16)

scenes.title: Watch it
narration: Danced in a closed, offset position.
The basic step is a six-count pattern: slow (step-hop), slow (step-hop), quick (step), quick (step).
Dancers maintain a constant vertical pulse on the balls of their feet.
Watch for Sailor Steps, Shag Dips.
on_screen: Hero video full screen, 30–45 s (uUGsLoZYXb4)
Captions name each signature move as it appears
Formation: Closed, offset partner position.
scenes.music: diegetic (the video's own sound), underscore under narration

scenes.title: Listen
narration: Performed to uptempo swing and pre-swing jazz music, including Dixieland and Gypsy-Jazz.
The tempo is typically between 185 and 250+ beats per minute.
Listen for the Brass, Woodwinds, Piano, Double bass.
The pulse is 4/4 at about 217 beats a minute.
High-tempo jazz characterized by a driving, consistent beat that supports a constant vertical bounce in the dancers.

scenes.title: The people
narration: Ryan Martin, who released the 2014 film 'The Rebirth of Shag'.
Carolina Shag and St. Louis Shag are distinct dances that share the name but are not directly related to Collegiate Shag.
Part of the swing family of American vernacular dances; shares roots with other 1920s African American dances.

scenes.title: Body and posture
narration: Upright, constant vertical pulse on the balls of the feet.
Closed position with arms held high; lead's right hand on follow's back, follow's left arm on lead's shoulder.
Torso remains largely calm while legs perform rapid movements.
